title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate–Verify‑Repair for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks: a Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify‑repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM generates device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by baseline and guarded), N = 200 paired intents were executed across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns. Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference = 0.02; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (predeclared primary test). An archived paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04] (reported as exploratory distinct from the preregistered confirmatory test). Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, verifier traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation using large language models (LLMs) can reduce routine operator effort in network operations (NetOps) but faces concrete safety and correctness challenges: LLM outputs may contain syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes that have direct operational consequences (outages or mis‑provisioned access). Prior prototype studies show verifier‑assisted loops reduce mechanically checkable errors in constrained settings but leave open questions about scaling across heterogeneous vendor templates, the operational cost of repairs, and inference interpretation when paired comparisons reuse the same initial candidate [1]–[6].

We designed a preregistered paired experiment to answer a tightly scoped confirmatory question: does a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM repair budget reduce the per‑intent incidence of operationally detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation when the same initial model candidate is reused across arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics)? The study focuses on mechanically checkable violations (syntax, topology/reachability, and encoded ACL/policy constraints) where a deterministic validator can provide localized feedback and trigger at most one repair call per intent.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and recent NetOps studies report rapid growth of LLM‑for‑NetOps research and emphasize evaluation gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5],[6]. Prototype work demonstrates that LLMs can draft device configurations but commonly introduce syntax/topology or policy errors; closed‑loop generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipelines are a recurrent mitigation pattern and show empirical benefits in code and configuration‑like domains [2],[3].

However, prior demonstrations typically evaluate narrow device families or single‑router translations and often lack provenance‑traced paired designs that explicitly separate initial generation sampling from verifier/repair effects. Our study addresses this gap by executing a provenance‑traced, preregistered paired evaluation over multi‑vendor template families and topology patterns with deterministic validator traces recorded for every episode.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls. The primary estimand (confirmatory) is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the difference in probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable policy violations under guarded (GVR) minus baseline (single‑shot LLM). The preregistration, analysis plan, exclusion/missingness rules, and power rationale are archived (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50).

Sampling and pairing: N = 200 unique operator intents were selected deterministically and stratified across 3 vendor‑template families and 4 topology patterns (12 strata) per the preregistered task_index_profile. Episodes were paired (baseline, guarded) and executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this design baseline is defined as the validator score on that shared initial candidate and guarded is the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. Because the initial candidate is shared, any within‑pair difference can only arise from deterministic validation and the permitted verifier‑triggered repair; no independent first‑pass sampling differences between arms were executed.

Model, sampling, and temperature: The declared model identifier in the archived model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; explicitly, null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The preregistered budget constrained initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 with a maximum_model_calls = 400.

Validator and scoring: The deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 evaluates syntactic correctness, reachability/topology constraints via emulation traces, and encoded ACL/policy constraints derived from the task payload. The preregistered binary per‑intent scoring rule labels an episode as a "success" only when the final configuration passes the full intent constraint validation (no operationally detectable violations). Repair policy: the guarded pipeline permitted up to one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent; repair prompts were localized and derived from validator diagnostics. All validator traces, repair prompts, and final validation outcomes were archived per episode.

Statistical analysis: The preregistered primary test is an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired success indicators. Complementary exploratory analyses (predeclared) include a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation). The preregistered multiplicity plan declares the McNemar test as confirmatory and treats secondary/interval estimates as exploratory.

Accounting, missingness, and deviations: Exclusion and missingness rules in the preregistration were applied; no pairs were excluded. Provider accounting was audited during execution and is reported verbatim in Results. No post hoc changes to the primary estimand or the shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics were made.
sections.results:
Execution summary and provider accounting: The run completed as preregistered (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200). Audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposes to 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls (repair stage_count = 4). Cache accounting records cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 204 (audited manifest values).

Paired contingency and primary inference: The paired 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 0.125 (confirmatory inference; do not reject at α = 0.05).

Exploratory interval and cost metrics: The archived paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04] for the paired risk difference; per the preregistration this interval is exploratory. Cost accounting from audited model calls shows total hosted model calls = 204, mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02, mean extra calls per intent due to guarded repairs = 0.02, and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0 (4 repair calls corresponding to 4 baseline failures corrected by repairs).

Representative artifact diagnostics: Representative execution/responses and execution/scoring entries in the archived bundle show that for each reported discordant pair the baseline and guarded episodes share identical initial candidate content (shared_initial_candidate) and that repairs were invoked only when the deterministic validator flagged violations. Validator traces record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and validation_before/validation_after states; these artifacts substantiate the contingency counts and the repair-triggered corrections.

Statistical diagnostics and sparse‑discordance caution: The total number of discordant pairs (n10+n01 = 4) is small. In sparse‑discordance regimes exact conditional tests (McNemar) and resampling‑based intervals can give differing signals; accordingly we emphasize the preregistered McNemar test as the formal confirmatory outcome and treat the bootstrap CI as exploratory context.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs exploratory interpretation: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test is the study's formal confirmatory inference and did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). The point estimate (0.02) and the exploratory bootstrap CI provide effect‑magnitude context but cannot alter the preregistered confirmatory conclusion.

Design implications of shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both arms, observed paired improvements derive solely from deterministic validation and allowed repair. This choice intentionally isolates verifier/repair effectiveness from first‑pass sampling or prompt‑engineering differences; it does not permit attributing gains to constrained prompting or independent re‑sampling. No independent constrained‑prompt arm was executed in this run.

Operationally bounded implications and cost tradeoffs: In this emulated, template‑driven setting a very small repair budget (4 repairs over 200 intents) eliminated the mechanically detectable baseline violations in the archived workload at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02). This artifact‑grounded result suggests that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and yields actionable diagnostics, modest repair budgets can remove mechanically checkable faults in similar template‑based emulations. We do not claim production readiness or coverage of semantic correctness beyond the validator's rule set.

Threats to validity and generalization (expanded): Construct validity—the deterministic validator detects mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings) but cannot guarantee detection of higher‑order semantic misinterpretations outside its encoded rule set. External validity—the experiment used a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), Mininet‑style emulation, and synthetic vendor templates; results do not directly imply equivalent performance on production hardware, different models, or in‑field operator workflows. Internal validity—the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics prevent attributing improvements to prompt engineering or independent sampling; this was intentional but limits the set of causal claims attributable to prompting choices. Conclusion validity—the low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduces power to detect small absolute improvements; sparse discordant counts can make interval estimators unstable. These limitations are enumerated in the Disclosure and Limitations sections and are supported by archived execution artifacts.

Recommendations and prioritized next steps grounded in archived evidence: expand validator coverage to include structured semantic/policy ontologies; evaluate GVR across multiple hosted models and provider versions to profile robustness to provider nondeterminism; and preregister independent multi‑sample baseline arms if the research question targets prompt/prompt‑engineering effects rather than verifier/repair effects. Each recommendation is predicated on archived artifact observations (low repair count, shared candidate semantics, and validator trace structure) and should be implemented with provenance‑traced preregistration.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) measuring whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact McNemar two‑sided) did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04]. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that, when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in this emulated template‑based setting. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator; further preregistered, multivendor/hardware evaluations with expanded verifier coverage are required.

disclosure_statement: Declared artifacts and autonomy: declared model gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; synthetic Mininet‑style harness. Preregistration: study preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) prior to any model calls. Initial master prompt: immutable initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Autonomy boundary and human role: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the lock the AI autonomously performed literature verification, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting. Generation semantics and temperature: execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by baseline and guarded; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1); the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed to 200 shared initial generation events + 4 verifier‑triggered repair calls. Reporting and provenance: reported counts and analysis artifacts are recorded in the archived execution and analysis bundles referenced above; no human manual editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements and makes interval estimators (bootstrap) potentially unstable in sparse‑discordance regimes.
